payload.holding: The High Court modified the Tribunal's award, holding that the Insurance Company must first pay the compensation amount to the claimant and then recover the same from the insured owner due to breach of policy conditions regarding the driver's license.
payload.ratio: Where the driver of a transport vehicle holds only a light motor vehicle licence without the specific authorisation or badge required to drive a transport vehicle, there is a breach of policy conditions permitting the insurer to pay the third-party compensation first and subsequently recover the amount from the insured owner.

payload.court: In The High Court Of Karnataka At Bengaluru
payload.holding: The Court held that where a driving license is renewed more than 30 days after its expiry, it takes effect from the date of renewal and does not cover the interregnum period of the accident, but directed the insurance company to satisfy the award and recover the amount from the insured owner under the 'pay and recover' principle.
payload.ratio: When an application for renewal of a driving license is made more than 30 days after its expiry, the license is renewed from the date of renewal; thus, the driver does not hold a valid license on the date of an accident occurring during the lapsed period, absolving the insurer of primary liability, though a 'pay and recover' order may be issued in favour of third-party claimants.

payload.title: K.G. Srinivasamurthy vs Habib Khathun And Ors.
payload.holding: The court held that the insurance companies were jointly and severally liable with the owners to satisfy the third-party claims despite the drivers' licences not being current on the exact date of the accidents, and enhanced the compensation awarded in both claim cases while reducing the interest rate to 9% per annum.
payload.ratio: The insurer is statutorily liable to satisfy an award obtained by a third party under the Motor Vehicles Act regardless of any policy condition breaches such as an expired driving licence, and the mere non-renewal of an otherwise valid licence on the date of the accident does not constitute a fundamental breach absolving the insurer of its third-party liability.

More often than not, literal interpretation of a statute or a provision of a statute results in absurdity.
Therefore, while interpreting statutory provisions, the Courts should keep in mind the objectives or
purpose for which statute has been enacted. Justice Frankfurter of U.S. Supreme Court in an article
titled as Some Reflections on the Reading of Statutes (47 Columbia Law Reports 527), observed that,
"legislation has an aim, it seeks to obviate some mischief, to supply an adequacy, to effect a change
of policy, to formulate a plan of Government. That aim, that policy is not drawn, like nitrogen, out of
the air; it is evidenced in the language of the statutes, as read in the light of other external
manifestations of purpose".

The inevitable conclusion therefore is that the decision in Swaran Singh's case (supra) has no
application to own damage cases. The effect of fake license has to be considered in the light of what
has been stated by this Court in New India Assurance Co., Shimla v. Kamla and Ors. (2001 (4) SCC
342). Once the license is a fake one the renewal cannot take away the effect of fake license. It was
observed in Kamla's case (supra) as follows:
"12. As a point of law we have no manner of doubt that a fake licence cannot get its
forgery outfit stripped off merely on account of some officer renewing the same with
or without knowing it to be forged. Section 15 of the Act only empowers any Licensing
Authority to "renew a driving licence issued under the provisions of this Act with
effect from the date of its expiry". No Licensing Authority has the power to renew a
fake licence and, therefore, a renewal if at all made cannot transform a fake licence as
genuine. Any counterfeit document showing that it contains a purported order of a
statutory authority would ever remain counterfeit albeit the fact that other persons
including some statutory authorities would have acted on the document unwittingly
on the assumption that it is genuine".

supporting.quote: When an owner is hiring a driver he will therefore have to check whether the driver has a driving licence. If the driver produces a driving licence which on the face of it looks genuine, the owner is not expected to find out whether the licence has in fact been issued by a competent authority or not. The owner would then take the test of the driver. If he finds that the driver is competent to drive the vehicle, he will hire the driver.

supporting.title: United India Insurance Company Limited vs V.Vijayakumar
supporting.principle: The insurer must prove that the insured was guilty of negligence and failed to exercise reasonable care in fulfilling the policy condition regarding use of vehicles by a duly licensed driver. The burden of proving breach is on the insurer.
supporting.fact_alignment: The driver held only an LMV licence without the badge/authorisation to drive a transport vehicle. The court examined whether the insurer had proved breach by the owner.
supporting.why_it_matters: This judgment (citing Swaran Singh) establishes that the insurer cannot simply show the licence was invalid — it must also prove the owner was negligent in failing to check. The burden of proof is squarely on the insurer.
supporting.quote: The breach of policy condition e.g. disqualification of the driver or invalid driving licence of the driver, as contained in sub-section (2)(a)(ii) of Section 149, has to be proved to have been committed by the insured for avoiding liability by the insurer. ... To avoid its liability towards the insured, the insurer has to prove that the insured was guilty of negligence and failed to exercise reasonable care in the matter of fulfilling the condition of the policy regarding use of vehicles by a duly licensed driver.

supporting.title: S.Iyyapan vs M/S United India Insurance Co.Ld.& Anr
supporting.principle: An insurer cannot avoid its statutory liability to pay compensation to third parties merely because the driver of a light motor vehicle did not have a specific endorsement to drive it as a commercial vehicle.
supporting.fact_alignment: The driver held a valid LMV licence but lacked a commercial endorsement for a Maxi Cab. The Supreme Court held the insurer liable to third parties.
supporting.why_it_matters: This limits the scope of licence defects that can defeat the insurer's defence. A missing endorsement for a commercial vehicle when the driver holds the underlying class licence does not let the insurer off the hook for third-party claims.
supporting.quote: Merely because the driver did not get any endorsement in the driving licence to drive Mahindra Maxi Cab, which is a light motor vehicle, the High Court has committed grave error of law in holding that the insurer is not liable to pay compensation because the driver was not holding the licence to drive the commercial vehicle.

supporting.title: Satto & Ors vs New India Assurance Co Ltd
supporting.principle: The breach must be conscious and wilful on the part of the insured. Even if a conscious breach is established, the insurer has a statutory liability to pay the third party and can only recover from the insured.
supporting.fact_alignment: The driver possessed only an LMV (non-transport) licence but was driving a goods vehicle. The insurer proved the breach but was still ordered to pay and recover.
supporting.why_it_matters: Reinforces that the insurer's defence of licence defect does not defeat the third-party claim — it only entitles the insurer to pay-and-recover. The breach must be conscious and wilful by the owner.
supporting.quote: It is well settled that the breach must be conscious and wilful. Even if a conscious breach on the part of the insured is established, still the insurer has a statutory liability to pay the compensation to the third party and will simply have the right to recover the same from the insured/tortfeasor.

supporting.title: United India Insurance Co Ltd., vs Smt Parvathi Hebbar
supporting.principle: The owner has a responsibility under Section 5 of the MV Act to see that no vehicle is driven by a person who does not satisfy Sections 3 or 4. However, even where the licence had lapsed, the insurer must pay the third party and recover from the owner.
supporting.fact_alignment: The driver's licence had expired before the accident and was renewed only after the accident. The court held the driver did not hold a valid licence on the accident date.
supporting.why_it_matters: Confirms that even where the owner entrusted the vehicle to a person without a valid licence (expired licence), the insurer's remedy is pay-and-recover, not outright avoidance of liability to the third party.
supporting.quote: The owner of motor vehicle, in terms of Section 5 of the Act, has a responsibility to see that no vehicle is driven by a person, who does not satisfy the provisions of Sections 3 or 4 of the Act.

supporting.title: United India Insurance Company Ltd vs Neelam Devi And Others
supporting.principle: Where a special endorsement is required (e.g., for carrying hazardous goods), the owner has a duty under Rule 132(5) of the CMVR to ensure the driver holds the requisite endorsement. Absence of such endorsement is a breach entitling the insurer to pay and recover.
supporting.fact_alignment: The vehicle was a tanker carrying hazardous goods. The driver held a licence for HGV/HTV but lacked the special endorsement required under Rule 9 read with Rule 132 of the CMVR.
supporting.why_it_matters: Establishes that for specialised vehicles (hazardous goods), the owner's duty is higher — the owner must ensure the driver has the specific regulatory endorsement. Failure is a breach, but still results in pay-and-recover, not insurer exoneration.
supporting.quote: As per Rule 132 (5) of Central Motor Vehicles Rule, 1989, it is the duty of the owner to ensure that the driver of the goods carriage carrying dangerous or hazardous goods holds a driving license as per the rule 9 of the aforesaid Central Motor Vehicles Rules.

adverse.title: Sunil Shreesail Killiket vs Subbraya
adverse.principle: Driving a motor vehicle without a valid licence constitutes a fundamental and statutory breach of the insurance policy, absolving the insurer of direct liability.
adverse.risk_to_client: The insurer will argue that where the driver had no licence at all (not merely a defective or expired one), the breach is so fundamental that even the pay-and-recover principle should not apply, and the owner alone should bear the entire liability.
adverse.distinguishing_argument: This is a Tribunal decision, not binding on higher courts. Moreover, the judgment itself ultimately ordered pay-and-recover (not exoneration of the insurer), citing Amrit Paul Singh v. TATA AIG. The 'fundamental breach' language was used to describe the owner's liability to indemnify the insurer, not to defeat the third-party claim. The insurer was still directed to pay first.
adverse.quote: It is held that as rightly argued by the learned counsel for the respondent No.2 the respondent No.1 has breached the fundamental condition of the policy by allowing the driver who has no driving licence to drive the vehicle.

adverse.title: National Insurance Co. Ltd vs Laxmi Narain Dhut
adverse.principle: The Swaran Singh principles (including pay-and-recover) apply only to third-party claims, not to own-damage claims. A fake licence cannot be cured by subsequent renewal.
adverse.risk_to_client: The insurer will argue that if the claim is for own damage (not third-party), the owner's failure to verify a fake licence means the insurer owes nothing at all — no pay-and-recover, no liability.
adverse.distinguishing_argument: This case is expressly limited to own-damage/non-third-party claims. For third-party injury/death claims (which are the vast majority of motor accident cases), Swaran Singh and the pay-and-recover principle continue to apply. The distinction is critical: this judgment helps the insurer only in own-damage or consumer forum disputes.
adverse.quote: The decision in Swaran Singh's case (supra) has no application to cases other than third party risks. ... Where originally the license was a fake one, renewal cannot cure the inherent fatality.

adverse.title: K.G. Srinivasamurthy vs Habib Khathun And Ors.
adverse.principle: Where a licence had expired before the accident and was renewed only after the accident, the renewal takes effect from the date of renewal, not retrospectively, so the driver did not hold a valid licence on the accident date.
adverse.risk_to_client: The insurer will argue that an expired licence is equivalent to no licence, and the owner should have checked that the licence was current on the date of employment and on each day of driving.
adverse.distinguishing_argument: This judgment actually held the insurer liable to the third party despite the expired licence, finding no wilful breach by the owner. The court distinguished between 'no licence at all' and 'licence that had lapsed but was subsequently renewed'. The latter does not defeat the third-party claim.
adverse.quote: The drivers who had not got their licences renewed on the date of accident do not stand on the same footing as the persons who did not have any licence at all or the persons who had driving licence which had expired and had never got it renewed.

adverse.title: Kamal S/O Shiv Ram vs Mursleem S/O Mohd. Akil
adverse.principle: Driving without a valid licence can constitute contributory negligence, reducing the claimant's compensation.
adverse.risk_to_client: The insurer will argue that if the injured claimant himself was driving without a licence, his own negligence contributed to the accident, reducing the award by up to 50%.
adverse.distinguishing_argument: This applies only where the claimant/victim was the unlicensed driver, not where the owner employed an unlicensed driver who injured a third party. It is a contributory negligence case, not a licence-verification case.
adverse.quote: The contributory negligence of injured is proved in view of testimony of PW-1 Kamal who categorically deposed ... he did not have DL at the time of accident ... 50% of the total compensation amount is deducted towards contributory negligence.

adverse.title: National Insurance Company Ltd. Thr. ... vs Smt. Meena And 4 Others
adverse.principle: Where the owner fails to produce the driver's licence or evidence of verification, an adverse inference may be drawn that the owner did not exercise reasonable care.
adverse.risk_to_client: The insurer will argue that the owner's failure to lead evidence about checking the licence means the court should infer the owner was negligent, defeating the owner's defence.
adverse.distinguishing_argument: The burden of proving breach remains on the insurer. The owner's silence does not automatically discharge that burden. Moreover, in Chennamma (doc_027), the owner remained ex-parte but the court still held the insurer liable to pay and recover, not to avoid liability entirely.

priority_arguments: The owner's duty is limited: check the licence on its face (looks genuine? yes), take a test drive (driver competent? yes). If both conditions are satisfied, the owner has discharged the duty and there is no 'breach' by the insured under Section 149(2)(a)(ii).

The burden of proving breach is on the insurer. Mere absence, fake, or invalid licence does not automatically defeat the insurer's liability — the insurer must prove the owner was negligent or knew of the defect.

Even if breach is proved (conscious and wilful), the insurer's remedy is pay-and-recover, not outright avoidance of liability to the third party. The third-party victim cannot be made to suffer for the owner's breach.
A missing endorsement (e.g., commercial vehicle badge on an LMV licence) is not a fundamental breach — S.Iyyapan holds the insurer liable despite this.
An expired licence that is subsequently renewed does not equate to 'no licence at all' — the driver had held a licence and was not disqualified from holding one.
strategy.compensation_range: Not applicable — this is a liability/defence question, not a quantum question.
risks: If the driver had no licence at all (never held one), the breach is more serious and some Tribunals may resist pay-and-recover (see doc_024), though the better view is that pay-and-recover still applies.
For own-damage claims (not third-party), Laxmi Narain Dhut (doc_031) holds that Swaran Singh does not apply and a fake licence defeats the claim entirely.
If the owner cannot produce any evidence of having checked the licence (e.g., no record, owner ex-parte), the court may draw an adverse inference, making it harder to resist the insurer's case.
For specialised vehicles (hazardous goods tankers), the owner's duty is higher — the owner must ensure the driver holds the specific regulatory endorsement under Rule 132 CMVR.
strategy.recommended_forum_or_relief: For third-party claims: argue that the insurer must pay first and can only seek recovery from the owner. The owner should lead evidence of having checked the licence (even a simple statement that the driver produced a licence that looked genuine and the owner took a test drive). For own-damage claims: the position is weaker — the owner must prove the licence was valid, not just that it looked genuine.

caveats: This corpus does not contain the full text of National Insurance Co. Ltd. v. Swaran Singh (2004) 3 SCC 297 or United India Insurance Co. Ltd. v. Lehru (2003) 3 SCC 338, which are the foundational Supreme Court authorities on this subject. They are cited extensively in the corpus judgments and their principles are applied, but the original texts are not available for direct quotation.

The corpus contains no judgment specifically on the 'fake licence' scenario where the owner checked a licence that appeared genuine but was later found to be forged. The closest is doc_027 (Chennamma) which quotes Lehru on this point: the owner is not expected to verify with the RTO.

doc_031 (Laxmi Narain Dhut) is an important limitation: Swaran Singh principles do not extend to own-damage claims. Practitioners must carefully distinguish between third-party and own-damage contexts.

doc_009 (Kamal) deals with contributory negligence of an unlicensed rider-claimant, not with the owner's duty to verify a driver's licence. It is included as adverse only because the insurer may cite it for the proposition that driving without a licence is negligence.

supporting.title: The Manager vs Chennamma

If the driver produces a licence that on its face looks genuine, the owner is not expected to find out whether the licence was actually issued by a competent authority. The owner would then take a test drive. If the owner is satisfied the driver is competent, there is no breach of Section 149(2)(a)(ii).

If the driver produces a driving licence which on the face of it looks genuine, the owner is not expected to find out whether the licence has in fact been issued by a competent authority or not. The owner would then take the test of the driver. If he finds that the driver is competent to drive the vehicle, he will hire the driver.
